paper.title: Implementation of altered provider incentives for a more individual-risk-based assignment of dental recall intervals: evidence from a health systems reform in Denmark
paper.code_data_availability: No data or code availability statement is printed. The paper states: …

registers.name_in_paper: the Danish National Health Insurance database (administrative dental treatment claims, obtained from the Danish Health Authority)
registers.role: treatment (date of claim relative to the 1 April 2015 reform), outcomes (remunerated treatment codes), controls (patient age, sex, municipality), sample frame
variables_mentioned: municipality of both patient and dental practice

registers.name_in_paper: Statistikbanken.dk (StatBank Denmark), 'Income by municipality, unit, family type and income interval'
registers.role: controls / subgroup split: average income of the municipality in which the patient lives, used as a socio-economic-status proxy for dental disease risk
variables_mentioned: average income of the municipality in which the patient lives

linkages: claims are linked to patients through a pseudonymized patient identifier, which is what allows patient-level fixed effects: 'the multifactorial nature of the data allowed an exact matching of patients and treatments' (p. 485)
claims within a day are aggregated into a treatment session: 'one session consists of several treatments, all performed within a day' (p. 479)
patients are linked to municipal average income via their municipality of residence, assuming 'that patients usually seek dental care close to where they are living' (p. 480)

sample.universe: all treatment claims submitted by dental practitioners to the Danish National Health Insurance in Denmark, 2012-2016 (adult dental care; care for persons under 18 is provided in public clinics)
sample.unit_of_observation: a claim handed into the health insurance by a dentist ('A single observation was formed by a claim handed into the health insurance by a dentist'); the regressions are run at the level of the treatment session (all treatments performed within a day), and Table 3 statistics at the level of the patient
selection_rules: all treatment claims in the Danish National Health Insurance database between 2012 and 2016 (72,155,539 claims from 3,759,721 unique patients in 25,533,311 distinct treatment sessions)
'We performed several sense checks to exclude observations with typing errors or missing commas' (p. 479)
main analyses restricted to one year before and after the reform, 'excluding yearly seasonal trends' (p. 480)
robustness check excluding the year 2015 altogether, comparing 19 months before and after the reform year (p. 480)
for the recall-interval statistics of Table 3: 'Patients with 0 visits to the dentist were not considered as their recall intervals can't be recovered with claims-data based observations' (p. 481)
sample.period: 2012-2016 (Figure 2 tick labels extend to 2017 and its caption says 'the period of 2012 to 2017')
sample.n_observations: 72,155,539 treatment claims in 25,533,311 distinct treatment sessions; the regressions use 5,420,552 (OLS), 3,181,824 (12 months pre/post) and 3,259,848 (19 months pre/post excluding 2015) sessions

construction_notes: 'The dental services under scrutiny were divided into several treatment baskets: preventive (IPT, see Figure 1), diagnostic (FE, SE and DE see Figure 1), scaling, X-ray, periodontal and fillings.' (p. 479)

'For each of these categories, a binary variable was set to 1 for a particular session (one session consists of several treatments, all performed within a day) if at least one corresponding code was remunerated in that session. Otherwise, it was set to 0.' (p. 479)

'total number of sessions' is the only non-binary outcome: 'mostly binary variables (except for “total number of sessions” which is a count variable)' (p. 481); Table 2 describes it as the mean number of yearly sessions (2.41, SD 0.74)
'dental recalls were defined as treatment sessions which only included only SE and/or DE' (Table 3 note, p. 481)
socio-economic status proxy: average income of the municipality in which the patient lives (Statistikbanken.dk, 2017), median split
age risk proxy: median split of patient age at age 51
treatment-experience risk proxy: previous receipt of fillings or periodontal treatment ('0 treatments = low risk')
'Note that all treatment codes were changed with the introduction of the regulatory changes (only exception: code for preventive treatment).' (p. 485)

the fixed-effects models use no additional controls: 'we did not use additional controls as no time-varying confounders could be identified (we tried to control for age, but this did not add explanatory power)' (Table 4/5 notes)

claims.statement: The 2015 Danish dental care reform decreased total number of sessions (OLS with age, sex, municipality and time controls).

register_source.value: Danish National Health Insurance database: date of treatment of the claim relative to 1 April 2015 (no Statistics Denmark register is named)

definition.value: the '2015 reform': the collective agreement in force from April 1, 2015, negotiated between the Danish Regions and the Danish Dental Association and incorporating the Danish Health Authority's 2013 guidelines for dental recall intervals. Dentists must risk-classify every patient as green (healthy), yellow (at risk) or red (high risk); remuneration of Individual Preventive Treatment (IPT) in diagnostic check-ups and of the new Focused Examination (FE) code is restricted to yellow and red patients. In the regressions it enters as a binary regressor: 'the binary variable reform is 1 if an observation pertains to the period after the reform and 0 otherwise', together with a reform x time interaction.

timing.value: 1 April 2015 onwards: the reform dummy is 1 for sessions in the period after the reform, 0 before; the underlying guidelines were issued in 2013 and the collective agreement negotiated in 2014

register_source.value: Danish National Health Insurance database: remunerated treatment codes in a claim, aggregated to the treatment session (no Statistics Denmark register is named)

definition.value: count variable (the only non-binary outcome: 'independent, mostly binary variables (except for “total number of sessions” which is a count variable)'); Table 2 describes it as the mean number of yearly sessions (2.41) per patient, a session being all treatments performed within a day

timing.value: measured at the level of the treatment session on the date of the session; 2012-2016; the column header states no period restriction (the paper says the main analyses were restricted to one year before and after the reform, but 5,420,552 sessions exceed the 3,181,824 of the 12-month fixed-effects column)

units.value: number of treatment sessions (count variable)

magnitude.interpretation: 'The total number of sessions did only change marginally' (p. 481)

estimand.target_population: dental treatment sessions of adult patients in Denmark around the 1 April 2015 reform; every unit is exposed to the reform, so the estimate is for the treated population itself
estimand.formal_query: E[Y | do(reform=1)] - E[Y | do(reform=0)] for dental treatment sessions

population.description: all treatment sessions of adult dental patients in Denmark recorded as claims in the Danish National Health Insurance database that enter this regression (5,420,552 sessions)
population.ages: adults (dental care for adults; for persons under 18 care is provided in public dental clinics); mean age of patients 49.4 years (SD 16.9)
population.period: 2012-2016; the column header states no period restriction (the paper says the main analyses were restricted to one year before and after the reform, but 5,420,552 sessions exceed the 3,181,824 of the 12-month fixed-effects column)
subgroups_defined: socio-economic status proxy: median split on municipality average income; 'high risk' = lower-income half
age proxy: median split at age 51; 'high risk' = the older half
previous treatment experience: prior fillings or periodontal treatment = 'proxied high-risk group'
population.selection: sessions/claims are observed only for patients who attended a private dental practitioner and for whom a claim was submitted to the National Health Insurance; the data are nationwide ('all 72 million treatments carried out in Denmark from 2012 to 2016') and the authors state the analyses 'do not suffer from pitfalls related to sampled data such as selection bias, entirely eliminating the need of extrapolating statements to a larger population'

identification.source_of_variation: The 2015 reform: the collective agreement on adult dental care in force from 1 April 2015 (Regionernes Lønningsog Taksnævn, 2014) incorporating the Danish Health Authority's 2013 recall-interval guidelines, which made risk classification (green/yellow/red) and the IPT/FE codes the basis of remuneration. The reform applies nationwide and at once, so the variation exploited is purely before/after 1 April 2015.

key_assumptions.assumption: Absent the 2015 reform, utilization of the treatment codes would have continued at its pre-reform level and trend, so the before/after contrast in the interrupted time series is the reform's effect.
key_assumptions.supported_by: the design is an interrupted time series ('we compared the utilization of dental services before and after the introduction of the reform using an interrupted time series design'); the main analyses are restricted to one year before and after the reform 'excluding yearly seasonal trends', and Figure 2 plots the monthly trajectories for 2012-2017 with a vertical line at April 1, 2015. No formal pre-trend test is reported.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on the observed controls (time, gender, age, municipality), the reform indicator is independent of the unobserved determinants of what a session contains.
key_assumptions.supported_by: table note: 'In our OLS model, we used age, sex and municipality of patients as confounders'; the authors add that 'if patient characteristics are not fully contained in the available explanatory variables, OLS regression models may be biased', which motivates the fixed-effects models

threats_discussed: seasonal trends in utilization (addressed by restricting the main analyses to one year before and after the reform)
anticipatory effects before implementation (addressed by the robustness check that excludes the year 2015 altogether)
unobserved patient heterogeneity and limited observable confounders in claims data (addressed with patient-level fixed effects)
dentists' misclassification of patients into risk groups (yellow categorizations given to obtain remuneration; inaccurate gingivitis criteria)
data entry mistakes after all treatment codes were changed at the reform, whose extent is 'difficult to determine'

robustness_checks: 19 months before vs. 19 months after the reform year 2015, excluding 2015 altogether (Table 4, fourth column)
sub-group fixed-effects regressions on three proxies for dental disease risk: municipality average income (median split), patient age (median split at 51) and previous treatment experience (Table 5)
age was tried as an additional control in the fixed-effects model but 'did not add explanatory power'
unresolved_confounders: detailed individual risk groupings (the actual green/yellow/red classifications) were not available for scientific evaluation, so the authors 'could not perform more detailed analyses within actual classifications of risk groups'
data entry mistakes in the treatment codes: 'given the absence of reliable reference values for dental diagnostics or treatment needs, the extent of such coding issues is difficult to determine'
no oral health outcome measures were available ('Another weakness of our study was the lack of suitable outcome measures')
for this OLS column: 'if patient characteristics are not fully contained in the available explanatory variables, OLS regression models may be biased'

estimator.value: OLS (linear interrupted time-series regression at session level with binary treatment variables; linear probability model for the binary outcomes)

estimation.specification: interrupted time series at session level; the printed estimating equation is 'y_t = β0 + β1(time)_t + β2(gender) + β3(age) + β4(municipality) + β5(reform) + β6(reform x time) + ε (OLS)' (unnumbered, p. 479)

source_table.value: Table 4, second column (OLS), p. 482

heterogeneity.dimension: socio-economic status proxy: median split on municipality average income; 'high risk' = lower-income half / socio-economic status proxy: median split on municipality average income; 'low risk' = higher-income half
heterogeneity.finding: 'Parameter estimates differed relatively little when differentiating between persons with high vs. low income although effects for codes related to preventive and diagnostic services were stronger for the high-risk group' (Table 5, p. 482-483)

heterogeneity.dimension: age proxy: median split at age 51; 'high risk' = the older half / age proxy: median split at age 51; 'low risk' = the younger half
heterogeneity.finding: 'the estimated effects of regulatory changes on utilization of preventive, diagnostic and scaling items are larger for persons with higher risk (older age) than for persons with lower risk (younger age) but all have the same sign' (Table 5, p. 482-483)

heterogeneity.dimension: previous treatment experience: prior fillings or periodontal treatment = 'proxied high-risk group' / previous treatment experience: no prior fillings or periodontal treatment = 'proxied lower risk group'
heterogeneity.finding: 'the most substantial differences in parameter estimates were found for the total number of treatment sessions (after regulatory changes: fewer sessions for high risk patients; more sessions for low risk patients), scaling (... nearly four-fold more sessions with scaling for low-risk than for high-risk patients), and fillings (... fewer fillings for high-risk patients but more fillings for low-risk patients)' (p. 482)

Table 4 and the body text label the coefficients '%-points' although the printed values are changes in the 0-1 proportion of sessions; the abstract reports the same preventive coefficient as '31.5%-points'.

ambiguities: The paper prints no standard errors, p-values or significance stars; statistical significance here is read off whether the printed 95% confidence interval excludes zero (evidence record of kind derivation).

Table 4 and the body text label the coefficients '%-points' although the printed values are changes in the 0-1 proportion of sessions; the abstract reports the same preventive coefficient as '31.5%-points'.

The baseline mean recorded is the Table 2 summary mean across all 25,533,311 treatment sessions of 2012-2016, not a pre-reform-only mean; the paper prints no pre-period mean of the regression outcomes.

Table 4 prints the OLS interval for the diagnostic code as '[-0.299; 0.297]'; the upper bound is transcribed as printed, but is almost certainly a typographical sign error for -0.297 (the point estimate is -0.298). Significance is therefore recorded as null rather than inferred from the printed interval.

The OLS column header states no period restriction and its N (5,420,552 sessions) exceeds the 12-month fixed-effects sample (3,181,824), so the period this column covers is not determinable from the paper.

population.ages: adults (dental care for adults; for persons under 18 care is provided in public dental clinics); mean age of patients 49.4 years (SD 16.9)
population.period: the 12 months before and the 12 months after the 1 April 2015 reform
subgroups_defined: socio-economic status proxy: median split on municipality average income; 'high risk' = lower-income half
age proxy: median split at age 51; 'high risk' = the older half
previous treatment experience: prior fillings or periodontal treatment = 'proxied high-risk group'
population.selection: sessions/claims are observed only for patients who attended a private dental practitioner and for whom a claim was submitted to the National Health Insurance; the data are nationwide ('all 72 million treatments carried out in Denmark from 2012 to 2016') and the authors state the analyses 'do not suffer from pitfalls related to sampled data such as selection bias, entirely eliminating the need of extrapolating statements to a larger population'

identification.source_of_variation: The 2015 reform: the collective agreement on adult dental care in force from 1 April 2015 (Regionernes Lønningsog Taksnævn, 2014) incorporating the Danish Health Authority's 2013 recall-interval guidelines, which made risk classification (green/yellow/red) and the IPT/FE codes the basis of remuneration. The reform applies nationwide and at once, so the variation exploited is purely before/after 1 April 2015.

key_assumptions.assumption: Absent the 2015 reform, utilization of the treatment codes would have continued at its pre-reform level and trend, so the before/after contrast in the interrupted time series is the reform's effect.
key_assumptions.supported_by: the design is an interrupted time series ('we compared the utilization of dental services before and after the introduction of the reform using an interrupted time series design'); the main analyses are restricted to one year before and after the reform 'excluding yearly seasonal trends', and Figure 2 plots the monthly trajectories for 2012-2017 with a vertical line at April 1, 2015. No formal pre-trend test is reported.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on patient-level fixed effects (and the post-reform time trend), the reform indicator is independent of the unobserved determinants of what a session contains: the authors state that no time-varying confounders could be identified.
key_assumptions.supported_by: 'we exploited the longitudinal character of our data and included patient-level fixed effects, giving us the most complete control for unobserved heterogeneity'; table note: 'we did not use additional controls as no time-varying confounders could be identified (we tried to control for age, but this did not add explanatory power)'

key_assumptions.assumption: The claim-code measures are comparable before and after the reform even though 'all treatment codes were changed with the introduction of the regulatory changes (only exception: code for preventive treatment)', and coding error does not generate the estimated shifts.
key_assumptions.supported_by: the authors argue that by design 'there was no possibility for dentists to be slow in changing towards the new taxonomy of treatment codes', but concede 'data entry mistakes could still be a relevant issue' whose extent 'is difficult to determine'

key_assumptions.assumption: The analysis conditions on a dental session having taken place (a claim being submitted), which the reform itself may affect: session-level outcomes exist only for attenders.

definition.value: the '2015 reform': the collective agreement in force from April 1, 2015, negotiated between the Danish Regions and the Danish Dental Association and incorporating the Danish Health Authority's 2013 guidelines for dental recall intervals. Dentists must risk-classify every patient as green (healthy), yellow (at risk) or red (high risk); remuneration of Individual Preventive Treatment (IPT) in diagnostic check-ups and of the new Focused Examination (FE) code is restricted to yellow and red patients. In the regressions it enters as a binary regressor: 'the binary variable reform is 1 if an observation pertains to the period after the reform and 0 otherwise', together with a reform x time interaction.

timing.value: 1 April 2015 onwards: the reform dummy is 1 for sessions in the period after the reform, 0 before; the underlying guidelines were issued in 2013 and the collective agreement negotiated in 2014

register_source.value: Danish National Health Insurance database: remunerated treatment codes in a claim, aggregated to the treatment session (no Statistics Denmark register is named)

definition.value: binary indicator: 'equals 1 if fillings were remunerated in a particular session', otherwise 0

timing.value: measured at the level of the treatment session on the date of the session; not stated for the subgroup regressions; the table-level N equals that of the 12-months-pre/post fixed-effects column of Table 4

units.value: change in the proportion of treatment sessions containing the code (0-1 share of sessions); the paper labels these coefficients '%-points'

estimand.target_population: dental treatment sessions of the higher-income half of a median split on the socio-economic-status proxy (average income of the patient's municipality of residence); higher socio-economic status is taken to mean lower dental disease risk
estimand.time_horizon: not stated; the subgroup N (3,181,824 sessions) equals the 12-months-pre/post sample of Table 4
estimand.formal_query: E[Y | do(reform=1)] - E[Y | do(reform=0)] for dental treatment sessions of the higher-income half of a median split on the socio-economic-status proxy (average income of the patient's municipality of residence); higher socio-economic status is taken to mean lower dental disease risk

population.description: treatment sessions of the higher-income half of a median split on the socio-economic-status proxy (average income of the patient's municipality of residence); higher socio-economic status is taken to mean lower dental disease risk
population.ages: adults (dental care for adults; for persons under 18 care is provided in public dental clinics); mean age of patients 49.4 years (SD 16.9)
population.period: not stated for the subgroup regressions; the table-level N equals that of the 12-months-pre/post fixed-effects column of Table 4
subgroups_defined: socio-economic status proxy: median split on municipality average income; 'low risk' = higher-income half
population.selection: sessions/claims are observed only for patients who attended a private dental practitioner and for whom a claim was submitted to the National Health Insurance; the data are nationwide ('all 72 million treatments carried out in Denmark from 2012 to 2016') and the authors state the analyses 'do not suffer from pitfalls related to sampled data such as selection bias, entirely eliminating the need of extrapolating statements to a larger population'

identification.source_of_variation: The 2015 reform: the collective agreement on adult dental care in force from 1 April 2015 (Regionernes Lønningsog Taksnævn, 2014) incorporating the Danish Health Authority's 2013 recall-interval guidelines, which made risk classification (green/yellow/red) and the IPT/FE codes the basis of remuneration. The reform applies nationwide and at once, so the variation exploited is purely before/after 1 April 2015.

key_assumptions.assumption: Absent the 2015 reform, utilization of the treatment codes would have continued at its pre-reform level and trend, so the before/after contrast in the interrupted time series is the reform's effect.
key_assumptions.supported_by: the design is an interrupted time series ('we compared the utilization of dental services before and after the introduction of the reform using an interrupted time series design'); the main analyses are restricted to one year before and after the reform 'excluding yearly seasonal trends', and Figure 2 plots the monthly trajectories for 2012-2017 with a vertical line at April 1, 2015. No formal pre-trend test is reported.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on patient-level fixed effects (and the post-reform time trend), the reform indicator is independent of the unobserved determinants of what a session contains: the authors state that no time-varying confounders could be identified.
key_assumptions.supported_by: 'we exploited the longitudinal character of our data and included patient-level fixed effects, giving us the most complete control for unobserved heterogeneity'; table note: 'we did not use additional controls as no time-varying confounders could be identified (we tried to control for age, but this did not add explanatory power)'

given: patient time-invariant unobserved heterogeneity (patient fixed effect)

implies_edges.from: patient time-invariant unobserved heterogeneity (patient fixed effect)

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: sessions before 1 April 2015 are unaffected by the reform, although the underlying guidelines date from 2013 and the agreement was negotiated in 2014.
key_assumptions.supported_by: the robustness check that excludes the reform year: 'we chose to exclude the year 2015 from our analyses altogether and subsequently compared utilization in the 19 months before and after the reform year 2015, excluding anticipatory effects'

implies_edges.from: anticipation of the reform before 1 April 2015

key_assumptions.assumption: The claim-code measures are comparable before and after the reform even though 'all treatment codes were changed with the introduction of the regulatory changes (only exception: code for preventive treatment)', and coding error does not generate the estimated shifts.
key_assumptions.supported_by: the authors argue that by design 'there was no possibility for dentists to be slow in changing towards the new taxonomy of treatment codes', but concede 'data entry mistakes could still be a relevant issue' whose extent 'is difficult to determine'

key_assumptions.assumption: The analysis conditions on a dental session having taken place (a claim being submitted), which the reform itself may affect: session-level outcomes exist only for attenders.
key_assumptions.supported_by: the unit of analysis is the claim/session ('A single observation was formed by a claim handed into the health insurance by a dentist'); for the recall statistics the paper states 'Patients with 0 visits to the dentist were not considered as their recall intervals can't be recovered with claims-data based observations'

implies_edges.from: attendance at a dental session (sample inclusion)

threats_discussed: seasonal trends in utilization (addressed by restricting the main analyses to one year before and after the reform)
anticipatory effects before implementation (addressed by the robustness check that excludes the year 2015 altogether)
unobserved patient heterogeneity and limited observable confounders in claims data (addressed with patient-level fixed effects)

robustness_checks: 19 months before vs. 19 months after the reform year 2015, excluding 2015 altogether (Table 4, fourth column)
sub-group fixed-effects regressions on three proxies for dental disease risk: municipality average income (median split), patient age (median split at 51) and previous treatment experience (Table 5)
age was tried as an additional control in the fixed-effects model but 'did not add explanatory power'
unresolved_confounders: detailed individual risk groupings (the actual green/yellow/red classifications) were not available for scientific evaluation, so the authors 'could not perform more detailed analyses within actual classifications of risk groups'
data entry mistakes in the treatment codes: 'given the absence of reliable reference values for dental diagnostics or treatment needs, the extent of such coding issues is difficult to determine'
no oral health outcome measures were available ('Another weakness of our study was the lack of suitable outcome measures')

estimator.value: linear individual (patient-level) fixed effects regression of an interrupted time series at session level, estimated on the subgroup

estimation.specification: interrupted time series at session level; the printed estimating equation is 'y_it = α_i + β(reform)_it + β(reform x time)_it + ε_it (Fixed Effects)' (unnumbered, p. 479)

sample_n.value: 3,181,824 (table-level N for all six subgroup columns; per-column N not printed)

source_table.value: Table 5, column 2 (proxy: income (median split @ income), low risk), p. 483

heterogeneity.dimension: socio-economic status proxy: median split on municipality average income; 'low risk' = higher-income half (contrast with the 'high risk' column)

heterogeneity.finding: 'By and large, the robustness checks neither provide clear evidence in support of, or against treatment patterns having become more risk-oriented in response to regulatory changes' (p. 482)

claims.statement: Comparing the periods before and after the 2015 Danish dental care reform, % of patients with a 6-month interval between dental recalls (or more frequently) increased.

register_source.value: Danish National Health Insurance database: whether a patient's claims fall before or after the 1 April 2015 reform (no Statistics Denmark register is named)

definition.value: the '2015 reform': the collective agreement in force from April 1, 2015, negotiated between the Danish Regions and the Danish Dental Association and incorporating the Danish Health Authority's 2013 guidelines for dental recall intervals. Dentists must risk-classify every patient as green (healthy), yellow (at risk) or red (high risk); remuneration of Individual Preventive Treatment (IPT) in diagnostic check-ups and of the new Focused Examination (FE) code is restricted to yellow and red patients. In the regressions it enters as a binary regressor: 'the binary variable reform is 1 if an observation pertains to the period after the reform and 0 otherwise', together with a reform x time interaction.

timing.value: Table 3 splits the 2012-2016 claims into 'before the 2015 reform' and 'after the 2015 reform'; the reform took effect on 1 April 2015

outcome.label: % of patients with a 6-month interval between dental recalls (or more frequently)

register_source.value: Danish National Health Insurance database: dates of the treatment sessions of each patient, from which visit and recall intervals are constructed

definition.value: share of patients whose interval between dental recalls is 6 months or shorter; 'dental recalls were defined as treatment sessions which only included only SE and/or DE'; patients with 0 visits were not considered

timing.value: per patient, averaged over the pre-reform and the post-reform period respectively

units.value: percentage points (change in the share of patients, in percent)

magnitude.interpretation: 'the proportion of patients with recall intervals of up to 6 months was by 1.2%-points larger post-implementation' (p. 480; also in the abstract)

estimand.target_population: the 3,759,721 unique patients with dental claims in the Danish National Health Insurance database, 2012-2016 (patients with 0 visits are not considered)
estimand.formal_query: E[Y | after the 2015 reform] - E[Y | before the 2015 reform]

population.ages: adults; mean age of patients 49.4 years (SD 16.9)
population.period: 2012-2016, split into before and after the 1 April 2015 reform
population.selection: patients are observed only through submitted claims; 'Patients with 0 visits to the dentist were not considered as their recall intervals can't be recovered with claims-data based observations'

identification.source_of_variation: The 2015 reform: the collective agreement on adult dental care in force from 1 April 2015 (Regionernes Lønningsog Taksnævn, 2014) incorporating the Danish Health Authority's 2013 recall-interval guidelines, which made risk classification (green/yellow/red) and the IPT/FE codes the basis of remuneration. The reform applies nationwide and at once, so the variation exploited is purely before/after 1 April 2015.

key_assumptions.assumption: Absent the 2015 reform, utilization of the treatment codes would have continued at its pre-reform level and trend, so the before/after contrast in the interrupted time series is the reform's effect.
key_assumptions.supported_by: the design is an interrupted time series ('we compared the utilization of dental services before and after the introduction of the reform using an interrupted time series design'); the main analyses are restricted to one year before and after the reform 'excluding yearly seasonal trends', and Figure 2 plots the monthly trajectories for 2012-2017 with a vertical line at April 1, 2015. No formal pre-trend test is reported.

key_assumptions.assumption: The raw pre/post comparison of Table 3 is not adjusted for patient composition or time trends; it assumes nothing else that moved between the two periods changed the statistic.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 3 reports pre- and post-reform averages only; no model, standard error or test is attached to them

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: sessions before 1 April 2015 are unaffected by the reform, although the underlying guidelines date from 2013 and the agreement was negotiated in 2014.
key_assumptions.supported_by: the robustness check that excludes the reform year: 'we chose to exclude the year 2015 from our analyses altogether and subsequently compared utilization in the 19 months before and after the reform year 2015, excluding anticipatory effects'

implies_edges.from: anticipation of the reform before 1 April 2015
implies_edges.to: % of patients with a 6-month interval between dental recalls (or more frequently)

key_assumptions.assumption: The claim-code measures are comparable before and after the reform even though 'all treatment codes were changed with the introduction of the regulatory changes (only exception: code for preventive treatment)', and coding error does not generate the estimated shifts.
key_assumptions.supported_by: the authors argue that by design 'there was no possibility for dentists to be slow in changing towards the new taxonomy of treatment codes', but concede 'data entry mistakes could still be a relevant issue' whose extent 'is difficult to determine'

key_assumptions.assumption: The analysis conditions on a dental session having taken place (a claim being submitted), which the reform itself may affect: session-level outcomes exist only for attenders.
key_assumptions.supported_by: the unit of analysis is the claim/session ('A single observation was formed by a claim handed into the health insurance by a dentist'); for the recall statistics the paper states 'Patients with 0 visits to the dentist were not considered as their recall intervals can't be recovered with claims-data based observations'

implies_edges.to: % of patients with a 6-month interval between dental recalls (or more frequently)

threats_discussed: seasonal trends in utilization (addressed by restricting the main analyses to one year before and after the reform)
anticipatory effects before implementation (addressed by the robustness check that excludes the year 2015 altogether)
unobserved patient heterogeneity and limited observable confounders in claims data (addressed with patient-level fixed effects)
dentists' misclassification of patients into risk groups (yellow categorizations given to obtain remuneration; inaccurate gingivitis criteria)
data entry mistakes after all treatment codes were changed at the reform, whose extent is 'difficult to determine'
no detailed individual risk-group information available, so risk-orientation of treatment could only be probed with proxies
robustness_checks: 19 months before vs. 19 months after the reform year 2015, excluding 2015 altogether (Table 4, fourth column)
sub-group fixed-effects regressions on three proxies for dental disease risk: municipality average income (median split), patient age (median split at 51) and previous treatment experience (Table 5)
age was tried as an additional control in the fixed-effects model but 'did not add explanatory power'
unresolved_confounders: detailed individual risk groupings (the actual green/yellow/red classifications) were not available for scientific evaluation, so the authors 'could not perform more detailed analyses within actual classifications of risk groups'
data entry mistakes in the treatment codes: 'given the absence of reliable reference values for dental diagnostics or treatment needs, the extent of such coding issues is difficult to determine'
no oral health outcome measures were available ('Another weakness of our study was the lack of suitable outcome measures')

claims.statement: Comparing the periods before and after the 2015 Danish dental care reform, average number of dental recalls per patient (per year) increased.

register_source.value: Danish National Health Insurance database: whether a patient's claims fall before or after the 1 April 2015 reform (no Statistics Denmark register is named)

definition.value: the '2015 reform': the collective agreement in force from April 1, 2015, negotiated between the Danish Regions and the Danish Dental Association and incorporating the Danish Health Authority's 2013 guidelines for dental recall intervals. Dentists must risk-classify every patient as green (healthy), yellow (at risk) or red (high risk); remuneration of Individual Preventive Treatment (IPT) in diagnostic check-ups and of the new Focused Examination (FE) code is restricted to yellow and red patients. In the regressions it enters as a binary regressor: 'the binary variable reform is 1 if an observation pertains to the period after the reform and 0 otherwise', together with a reform x time interaction.

timing.value: Table 3 splits the 2012-2016 claims into 'before the 2015 reform' and 'after the 2015 reform'; the reform took effect on 1 April 2015

outcome.label: Average number of dental recalls per patient (per year)

register_source.value: Danish National Health Insurance database: dates of the treatment sessions of each patient, from which visit and recall intervals are constructed

definition.value: mean number of dental recalls per patient per year; recalls are treatment sessions which only included SE and/or DE

timing.value: per patient, averaged over the pre-reform and the post-reform period respectively

units.value: recalls per patient per year

magnitude.interpretation: 'The average number of dentist visits and recalls per patient was shown to have increased slightly' (p. 480)

estimand.target_population: the 3,759,721 unique patients with dental claims in the Danish National Health Insurance database, 2012-2016 (patients with 0 visits are not considered)
estimand.formal_query: E[Y | after the 2015 reform] - E[Y | before the 2015 reform]

population.description: 3,759,721 unique patients with dental treatment claims in the Danish National Health Insurance database, 2012-2016 (Table 3 header: 'sample size: 3,759,721 unique patients')
population.ages: adults; mean age of patients 49.4 years (SD 16.9)
population.period: 2012-2016, split into before and after the 1 April 2015 reform
population.selection: patients are observed only through submitted claims; 'Patients with 0 visits to the dentist were not considered as their recall intervals can't be recovered with claims-data based observations'

identification.source_of_variation: The 2015 reform: the collective agreement on adult dental care in force from 1 April 2015 (Regionernes Lønningsog Taksnævn, 2014) incorporating the Danish Health Authority's 2013 recall-interval guidelines, which made risk classification (green/yellow/red) and the IPT/FE codes the basis of remuneration. The reform applies nationwide and at once, so the variation exploited is purely before/after 1 April 2015.

key_assumptions.assumption: Absent the 2015 reform, utilization of the treatment codes would have continued at its pre-reform level and trend, so the before/after contrast in the interrupted time series is the reform's effect.
key_assumptions.supported_by: the design is an interrupted time series ('we compared the utilization of dental services before and after the introduction of the reform using an interrupted time series design'); the main analyses are restricted to one year before and after the reform 'excluding yearly seasonal trends', and Figure 2 plots the monthly trajectories for 2012-2017 with a vertical line at April 1, 2015. No formal pre-trend test is reported.

key_assumptions.assumption: The raw pre/post comparison of Table 3 is not adjusted for patient composition or time trends; it assumes nothing else that moved between the two periods changed the statistic.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 3 reports pre- and post-reform averages only; no model, standard error or test is attached to them

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: sessions before 1 April 2015 are unaffected by the reform, although the underlying guidelines date from 2013 and the agreement was negotiated in 2014.
key_assumptions.supported_by: the robustness check that excludes the reform year: 'we chose to exclude the year 2015 from our analyses altogether and subsequently compared utilization in the 19 months before and after the reform year 2015, excluding anticipatory effects'

implies_edges.from: anticipation of the reform before 1 April 2015
implies_edges.to: Average number of dental recalls per patient (per year)

key_assumptions.assumption: The claim-code measures are comparable before and after the reform even though 'all treatment codes were changed with the introduction of the regulatory changes (only exception: code for preventive treatment)', and coding error does not generate the estimated shifts.
key_assumptions.supported_by: the authors argue that by design 'there was no possibility for dentists to be slow in changing towards the new taxonomy of treatment codes', but concede 'data entry mistakes could still be a relevant issue' whose extent 'is difficult to determine'

key_assumptions.assumption: The analysis conditions on a dental session having taken place (a claim being submitted), which the reform itself may affect: session-level outcomes exist only for attenders.
key_assumptions.supported_by: the unit of analysis is the claim/session ('A single observation was formed by a claim handed into the health insurance by a dentist'); for the recall statistics the paper states 'Patients with 0 visits to the dentist were not considered as their recall intervals can't be recovered with claims-data based observations'

threats_discussed: seasonal trends in utilization (addressed by restricting the main analyses to one year before and after the reform)
anticipatory effects before implementation (addressed by the robustness check that excludes the year 2015 altogether)
unobserved patient heterogeneity and limited observable confounders in claims data (addressed with patient-level fixed effects)
dentists' misclassification of patients into risk groups (yellow categorizations given to obtain remuneration; inaccurate gingivitis criteria)
data entry mistakes after all treatment codes were changed at the reform, whose extent is 'difficult to determine'
no detailed individual risk-group information available, so risk-orientation of treatment could only be probed with proxies
robustness_checks: 19 months before vs. 19 months after the reform year 2015, excluding 2015 altogether (Table 4, fourth column)
sub-group fixed-effects regressions on three proxies for dental disease risk: municipality average income (median split), patient age (median split at 51) and previous treatment experience (Table 5)
age was tried as an additional control in the fixed-effects model but 'did not add explanatory power'
unresolved_confounders: detailed individual risk groupings (the actual green/yellow/red classifications) were not available for scientific evaluation, so the authors 'could not perform more detailed analyses within actual classifications of risk groups'
data entry mistakes in the treatment codes: 'given the absence of reliable reference values for dental diagnostics or treatment needs, the extent of such coding issues is difficult to determine'
no oral health outcome measures were available ('Another weakness of our study was the lack of suitable outcome measures')
